utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is General Sir Rupert Smith. There is an application in respect of his witness statement that is before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we've seen the statement, and we've had the chance to consider it. What we would be minded to do is to admit the statement but require you, of course, to call evidence about -- live evidence about anything which is new, not in the statement, and also any matters of evidence relating to the accused, his acts and conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one meeting - I'll of course deal with that - one meeting directly with the accused. I'll get the witness to deal with that. There are two updated versions of the draft proofing document that you had. One is called "track changes," which will be familiar for those who work with the appropriate software, and therefore shows what is additional from the draft. One is free of track changes because some people find it inconvenient to work with track changes. I'm happy to work with whatever version is most convenient to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There is an issue of time, as far as this witness is concerned, because he is only here today, and we do not have this courtroom in the afternoon so we have to finish at the usual time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shall be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness come in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I would just like to say something very briefly. I respect, of course, what you've said just now, but it seems to me that the witness who is about to come in, General Rupert Smith, who was in 1991 commander over the UN Protection Forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina and who took over that duty on the 23rd of January, 1995, and then also throughout that year he carried out this duty all the way up to an action taken by NATO in the month of October, it seems to me that this is a witness who should perhaps be questioned in chief about all these relevant matters. It's not only relevant the fact that he had contacts with Slobodan Milosevic. He was one of the persons who followed all developments in 1995, which was an extremely important year. And I believe that there are many developments involved about which he should testify in chief, especially regarding everything that happened after Markale, after the 28th of August, 1995. I indeed believe that you should reconsider whether this is a witness who should be questioned in chief as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll reconsider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have considered this matter, and of course we've considered, the two of us, the arguments which Mr. Tapuskovic puts forward. We of course bear in mind the importance of the evidence which is to be given, but on the other hand, we have had benefit of argument yesterday, detailed arguments, which we've considered. Those arguments apply to this case. I should say that the original decision was the decision of the Trial Chamber as we considered it yesterday with Judge Robinson. Judge Kwon and I, of course, have reconsidered it now. We can see no reason to change our minds. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness come in. And in the absence of any indication to the contrary from the Chamber, I will use the updated summary that is not the "track changes" version, but I'm entirely in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Rupert Anthony Smith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Retired general of the British army, with a service history from 1964 covering experience in many theatres around the world, serving in the Gulf War, and involving yourself in the Balkans as early as late 1992 and early 1993 when you were in London at a desk position which gave you an overall view of the Balkans. Did you take command of the United Nations Protection Force in Bosnia-Herzegovina in January 1995, holding that position until December of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make a statement dated the 14th of August, 1996, to investigators of this Tribunal? Did you sign that statement? Have you reviewed it, and is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes to all of those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that statement, please, become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Kwon makes the point that we did not involve the -- yesterday, in yesterday's evidence, in the exhibit numbering, the binder of intercepts which the witness was about to produce. I don't know if we can do it this way, but it might be convenient if that is now given a number, albeit it will only be marked for identification, I suspect, and that has the next number which Judge Kwon has, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The intercept binder will be Exhibit 551, and the witness statement will be 552.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, there is a binder of exhibits to which the witness will refer but only briefly. May that be given the exhibit number 553.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concluding with your -- not concluding, but concluding the summary of your experience, General, following the position in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you command the British army, between 1996 and 1998? Did you then become Deputy Supreme Allied Commander Europe for NATO between 1998 and 2002?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Between 1996 and 1998 I commanded the British Armed Forces in Northern Ireland rather than the British army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: And yes, I was the Deputy Supreme Allied Commander Europe from 1998 to 2001, not 2. I retired in 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now on the revised summary at the first substantive page, page 3, paragraph 5. In the course of your duties in 1995, did you meet Karadzic, Mladic, and did you form any view from your dealings with them about their relationship with the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet both Karadzic and Mladic. The -- my views about Mladic's relationship with the accused was based on in some and in particular a meeting in July, but before that, there were examples for me where there were connections with Serbia and Milosevic. These were to do with the running of the Bosnian Serb forces and the state of their equipment, where they were getting ammunition from, and where they were being paid from, particularly the senior officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you form any view one way or the other as to whether Belgrade in general or the accused in particular had any influence over the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly had the view there was influence, yes, because they relied, that is the Bosnian Serbs, relied for support from the Serbian army or Serbian armed forces, and there was from their own account on occasions evidence that they were dealing with the General Staff and so forth in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 of the summary. As between Karadzic and Mladic, what did you infer to be the relationship in summary?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In sum, the -- Karadzic was the political leader and Mladic was the military leader. They stood together. They did this publicly as well as in more discrete forum when they were talking to me or Mr. Akashi, and the -- and Mladic made the point on plenty of occasions that he didn't do the politics. However, he drew a very wide definition of his military responsibilities, and he protected his right to direct and decide what happened in those from Karadzic and everybody else jealously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 9. As to whether there were any discussions on matters of strategy between Karadzic and Milosevic, your view and your view as to when if at all the accused elected to be involved.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think they undoubtedly, that is Karadzic and Mladic, discussed strategy and there was the case of a meeting in Jahorina where I am aware that that had actually happened in a more formal structure. The relationship with the accused, I think, was rather more that he interfered or became involved when the directions they were taking became counter to his interests and those of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 10. To what extent and in what way did the international community rely on or use the accused in respect of what they wanted from the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Because it was seen that Mr. Milosevic had influence over the Bosnian Serbs, the international community went to him and there is at least two occasions where we can see it happening, the recovery of hostages in May/June, and then during the Dayton talks, to bring as a route, as a source of influence and pressure over the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any, and if so which, senior VRS officers say anything to you about where they were paid and how?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't remember precisely who said it, but I think it was either Mladic or General Tolimir, but I was certainly told by one of them or another on at least one occasion that they were paid by Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the question of support, if any, from the FRY by way of ammunition, forces, mercenaries, et cetera, your experience.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: To an extent, the Bosnian Serb forces, particularly for specialist equipment or the repair and maintenance of bits of specialist equipment, relied on support from Belgrade, and the same applied to certain items of ammunition. The provision of supporting forces, I divide them up briefly into three groups. There were specials forces of the Serbian forces. There were, let's call it units of -- from Serbia such as Arkan's forces, and I was never quite clear exactly their relationships with the Serbian army, but they were formed bodies and recognisable. And then there were mercenary units in which it was alleged - I have no proof of this - that some of the people in them had come from Greece. I certainly saw evidence in the -- amongst the Serb forces and Bosnian Serb forces around Zepa of these reinforcing forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On an allied topic, paragraph 12 or the second part of paragraph 12, can you explain what you mean by an air defence system and give evidence of how you understood it to operate and what inferences you were to draw from NATO's attempts to destroy it.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: For an air defence system to work, you need what is referred to as a recognised air picture. This is collected and -- from a large number of sensors, radars, and so forth, and is disseminated widely, and the information is all collected together and fused into one picture. This defence system was set up in the time of Yugoslavia under Tito and didn't -- was not constructed on the basis of the boundaries of -- that existed in 1995. The -- and therefore, one must -- I was working on the assumptions that there was a feed of information that crossed all those boundaries from Serbia into Bosnia. This was demonstrated to me during the bombing of September when NATO was suppressing the air defence system as we knocked out the microwave towers over which this information is transmitted. They were in Bosnia. The Serbs continued -- the Bosnian Serbs continued to collect a recognised air picture, it being available through the linkages that were coming in from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that if you're right in the inference you draw, the feed came from an integrated system and knocking out the part in Bosnia didn't deny them a feed if it was coming from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Correct. And therefore, it was being managed and continued to be managed from within Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We move to the heading "Restriction on the enclaves," paragraph 14. On arrival -- actually, I think you covered this in your statement, so I needn't cover it. I'll move on to paragraph 15, which is the "Evidence of shift in RS military strategy." You had a series of meetings with Mladic in early March, but they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. are covered in your statement for the most part. However, at page -- paragraph 15 and onwards, you deal with something that was to become your thesis. Can you explain why it's necessary for you to form a thesis, or desirable; what your thesis was.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Forming a thesis is something I've learnt to do in these rather complex circumstances. It is -- it comes from having a thesis, then there's an antithesis, then there's a synthesis. My -- what I try to do is to arrive at a judgement. It doesn't -- from the information available to me, as to what is going to happen, what other people are going to do. I can then focus my collection of information to prove that or to disprove it, but also it allows me something to test the information that comes my way, to test that information against it and assess the information. By early to mid-March, I have been in command for approaching two months, and I've begun to form this view, a thesis as to what was about to happen, and that then became the testbed, if you like, against which I collected and assessed information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the thesis?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In sum, that the cessation of hostilities agreement was going to break down, that the parties to this conflict were intent on war, they needed to have a resolution by force by the end of 1995. From the Bosnian Serb point of view, that they had a shortage of manpower to defend the space they had, that if -- one of the ways of freeing up the available manpower, making more available, was to reduce the need to guard the three eastern enclaves, Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica. They also needed to keep the UN, because the UN was something of a protection against them being bombed by NATO. The -- and therefore, they would -- and I then deduced from that that therefore they would squeeze and bring pressure on the eastern enclaves in such a way that they neutralised their potential to the Bosnians as a source of military activity in the Bosnian Serb rear while keeping the UN in there so that they -- there was a hostage, as it were, to protect them from NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 18. Regardless of what was going to happen in the enclaves, your view on the significance of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I would make the point that Sarajevo was also an enclave. The -- and under siege. I considered Sarajevo was the decisive point, because some of the suburbs of Sarajevo were held by the Bosnian Serbs. The confrontation line ran through Sarajevo. Sarajevo was the capital, the seat of the Bosnian government. It was where the UN headquarters was. It was where the media were, and it was defended or guarded by a brigade found from a permanent member of the Security Council, France. For all of those reasons, it was a decisive point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 19. You had a meeting with Mladic on the 6th of March. It's dealt with in your statement. Tab 1 of Exhibit 553 is a record of that. Have you reviewed that exhibit? Does it faithfully set out the contents of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I've reviewed it, and yes, it does set out the contents of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph -- the follow-on paragraph is also covered in the statement, your original statement, but it's perhaps worth just underlining this point: At a meeting -- at the meeting that we've been dealing with, was Koljevic present?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he say, as your statement reveals, talking of people going to this Tribunal "If he goes, we all go and we don't mind how many go with us"?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then look, please, and this is only one of the two exhibits I'll ask the Chamber probably to look at, it's tab 2. If the witness can have it, and it's in the English version at page 10, and the last few lines of page 10. We may be able to display this on Sanction. I'm very grateful to Ms. Wee and indeed Ms. Edgerton for preparing the exhibits. Just, please, this document, General Smith, and then we'll look at the one. Perhaps it's highlighted.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Mine understanding -- I saw this document for the first time yesterday. My understanding of this document is it's a translation of a directive signed by Karadzic on the future strategic direction of the Bosnian Serb forces, and it appears to have been the results of this meeting at Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the passage we can see at the foot of page 10 reads in respect of the Drina Corps: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." And although I may not have asked Ms. Wee to prepare this, but if you go over in the original to page 11, you, I think, see some significance in the three lines at the top of page 11: "In case the UNPROFOR forces leave Zepa and Srebrenica, the DK command shall plan an operation named Jadar with the task of breaking up and destroying the Muslims forces in these enclaves and definitively liberating the Drina valley region." Your comment, please, on those two passages and how they affected your thesis.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The first extract, the last sentence of the first paragraph that we were shown, "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations ..." and then ending "... for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa," this I understand to be the -- the instructions to so squeeze and compress, both physically and in terms of a way of life, the existence of those enclaves. I do not see it because of this -- the second reference you made, the second paragraph, as an instruction to actually destroy them. They -- in the -- in that second paragraph, it -- the whole -- the whole instruction in that paragraph is dependent upon UNPROFOR leaving. It is only when the -- there is no reason for -- to keep the UN there because the UN have gone is that those enclaves are to be destroyed and done away with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I erred when I said it was only two exhibits. I'm going to ask you to look at three. The next one, please, is tab 3 but very briefly. Your comment on tab 3 which is a directive for further operations, again a document I think you've own seen recently, signed by Mladic and dated the 31st of March. Your comment on it in general terms, because I think it's a general comment that you can make.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. This, if you like, is a demonstration of Karadzic and Mladic working together. The first -- you can see the general directive by Karadzic, and it's then carried on with more specific instructions by Mladic to his forces, and a few days or weeks later -- I've got to look. Yes, it's about three weeks later, he issues a subsequent order clarifying or developing what the -- Karadzic had produced as the strategic direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Summary page 8, paragraphs 20 and 21, substantially covered in your statement. Your visit to Srebrenica on the 6th of March revealed - last line of paragraph 20 - on which some amplification - that every movement in and out of the enclave was checked and monitored by the Bosnian Serb checkpoint, and then this sentence, and there was "... the sense of being under the direct control of the VRS was palpable." Any further qualification for that and how general or long-standing that sense of VRS control was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It was deeply felt by the inhabitants of Srebrenica and by the unit DutchBat and the UNPROFOR forces that were in the pocket. I think it had been going on -- this was a developing sense that the longer you were there the longer and deeper this feeling pertained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be a tangential point, but in a sentence, in your judgement was the degree of VRS control over Srebrenica and the pockets properly broadcast around the world to different capitals or was it information that was for some reason or other not fully disseminated?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I do not think the circumstances in those enclaves, or to some extent in the whole of Bosnia, was properly understood in capitals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can amplify that, if asked, by anybody else. Paragraph 21. At the same time as you were rotating positions following General Rose, DutchBat was replacing a Canadian Battalion at Srebrenica. Had they been able to get all their weapons and ammunitions into the enclave or not?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, they had not. I can't remember the precise shortages, but there were shortages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 29 is dealt with in your statement, your meeting with Mladic on the 7th of March of 1995. As to paragraph 26, that is effectively dealt with in your statement save perhaps for the end. At this meeting, did Mladic express his views on the understanding of and size of enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. The -- this particular discussion started over a discussion as to the position of the UN observation posts on the south and south-east side of the Srebrenica pocket. Because of the positioning of these observation posts, it was Mladic's opinion that the Bosnians had been able to position their own lines so that they could interdict a road that was important to the Serbs that ran on an east-west access between Zepa and Srebrenica. He, Mladic, wanted me to reposition the OPs so as to allow Bosnian forces to drive the Muslims back and clear and allow the road -- better access to the road for the Bosnian Serbs. I refused to do this, and in this discussion it then became -- it was explained to me by Mladic that the boundaries we were occupying or that existed for these enclaves were not those that he, in his opinion, had agreed at the time of setting them up, and he drew on the map, sketched on the map where he thought those boundaries ought to be, the ones that he had agreed, and these were small lozenges around the actual built-up areas of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The exhibit formerly -- earlier tendered as Exhibit 546, tab 21, is one you've reviewed. Does that accurately set out the meeting of the 7th of March?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That's tab 21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, it's the earlier exhibit at the beginning of the binder and it's Exhibit 546.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 21, so it doesn't fall in the sequence of tabs.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, I have seen that, and yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 26 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. I'm not sure whether we received the witness's statement which is numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if you haven't had a numbered statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we haven't received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will have that corrected as soon as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My oversight. We'll send one up for copying now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 26 on page 9 of the supplement is dealt with in the statement. That's your meeting with Mr. Akashi when you went to Pale. Paragraph 28 is covered in your statement. Paragraph 30 -- I beg your pardon, paragraph 30 is covered in your statement. Paragraph 31, likewise, covered in your statement. Does tab 4 of the exhibit that's before you set out accurately the meeting -- the record of the meeting of the 5th of April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Yes. I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We move then to paragraph 32 in the summary on page 10. Meetings in Sarajevo and Pale on the 20th of April, covered in your witness statement and no need to go into those. Further meetings between the 30th of April and the 1st of May, covered in your statement in full. Perhaps worth observing in respect of the meeting on the 30th of April, paragraph 34 of the summary. This was where Karadzic is recorded as saying at one stage that if the international community treated Bosnian Serbs like beasts in a cage, that is how they would behave. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you reviewed tab 5 of the exhibit bundle? Notes of the meeting of the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that set out accurately what happened?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed we could find a passage in there where there's a reference to humanitarian and UNPROFOR convoys being said to be commercial convoys for the benefit of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 36 deals with following events in early May and is covered in your statement. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Paragraph 37 brings us to the 9th of May and your meeting then with Karadzic. Covered in your original statement, as indeed is your evidence that on the 16th and the 17th of May, serious fighting to the north-east and south-east of Sarajevo took place; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about those tanks that were involved in the fighting on the 16th and 17th of May? Where were they firing from? What were they doing that they shouldn't have been?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, they shouldn't have been firing because they were in the weapon collection point. I can't remember the precise details, but the -- these weapons were either taken or these tanks were either taken from the weapon collection point or manned and fired from within the weapon collection point. These weapons collection points it must be understood as quite wide areas and the weapons dispersed within them. It wasn't -- they weren't necessarily all in a hangar or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we've heard evidence about those weapon collection points already, so we move to paragraph 40, covered in your statement. But at 40 -- which is your meeting with Karadzic on the 21st of May. Paragraph 41. At that time, were you working or was UNPROFOR working on the thesis that the Bosnians were increasing their activity from the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I -- when I described the thesis, I -- for brevity, I only described the thesis from the point of view of the Bosnian Serbs, but the thesis also included that it was therefore in the interests of the Bosnian Muslims to conduct operations out of these enclaves so as to tie down as much Serb forces as possible, and that appeared to be happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you reviewed tab 6, and is that an accurate record of the meeting of the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have; and yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this stage was Sarajevo being shelled on a regular basis by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. It -- and this had been increasing, and from my memory, it had calmed down a little from the situation around the 16th, 17th but it had continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the principal targets? Paragraph 42, page 12.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- generally, the Jewish cemetery, the PTT building and the vicinity around there. The -- if you like, the front lines as well. And then we would also get them, rounds coming in around the old stadium at Zetra.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 43, page 13. Retaliatory shelling of Tuzla by the VRS. Can you tell us a little bit about that? On the 24th of May, did fighting flare up again, and did you take a decision and issue an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. We -- the shelling had continued during that month, and then it became more intense during the 24th, and weapons -- further weapons were taken from the weapon collection points, and at this point I issued an ultimatum during, if I remember correctly, the evening of the 24th, that if the weapons were not returned then NATO would be invited to carry out airstrikes. The weapons were not returned, and on the 25th, a target which was one of two bunkers in an ammunition dump near Pale was attacked by NATO. The response that evening was for the VRS to shell all the safe areas. The shelling of Tuzla killed 71 people in the marketplace that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tuzla, a safe area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meanwhile in Sarajevo, what was the position there, better, worse, or about the same?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that night it was --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Smith says the army of Republika Srpska shelled the area, and in translation that is being broadcast, an error was made and it was said that it was the army of the Republic of Serbia. So please could that error be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sarajevo, General.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- Sarajevo was also shelled, and the situation progressively deteriorated, but it didn't -- we bombed a second time, and the particular deterioration then occurred after that second bombing rather than after the first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to the taking of hostages, paragraph 46 and following. Can you give us in thumbnail outline the history of the taking of hostages?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, briefly. Almost immediately after the second airstrike, the UNMOs close that were -- lived in a house close to the Pale headquarters were seized and at least one, a Canadian, was chained to a bridge which was thought to be a potential target, and this was broadcast on television. I was rung up and threatened that if I didn't stop, he would be -- have his throat cut. And at the same time, we began to receive reports of other people being taken hostage in the Bosnian Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what extent was the taking of hostages and using of them as human shields widespread, and if so, what conclusions did you make as to coordination?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: There were some -- eventually there were some 400 people taken hostage. I can't remember at this range the -- precisely how many were taken in the sort of first tranche, but the seizure of hostages spread beyond the immediate vicinity of Pale and it was clearly directed from -- the directed action across the complete command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your witness statement deals with the contacts by phone you had with Mladic, your assertions, his counter-allegations. Did he maintain his right to keep these hostages and to use them in the way that you've described?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I -- without referring back to the statement, my memory is that he was intent on keeping the hostages and demanding that we ceased our actions altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosnian troops disguised as French soldiers, dealt with in your statement, as is the passage on the 28th of May where you had your final conversation with Mladic, informing him of the breach of Geneva Conventions in what he was doing. And does tab 7 summarise the document you've reviewed, summarise the telephone conversation that you had with him?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it does, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You refused further to negotiate with him. The pressure was brought to bear on the accused in this case. That's dealt with in your statement. Did you understand - paragraph 52 - that the accused did have a role in recovery of the hostages eventually?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- it was clear at the time that that was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 11, is that a document you've reviewed, and does that constitute a letter of complaint you sent on the 26th of June to Mladic about the shelling of the safe areas?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have reviewed it, and yes, it does that. It is a letter of complaint, protest even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other events in June of 1995. Was shelling and sniping taking place? What sort of regularity, if so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: At this range I have difficulty remembering -- yes, they were taking place, and I have difficulty in remembering its regularity. I think it -- I would use the word it was "normal." This had become the background to life in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ABiH attempt to break out of Sarajevo in June 1995 is dealt with in your statement, as is the appointment of Carl Bildt in place of Lord Owen to the European Union ICFY position. Did you have a meeting with him in June?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maintain contact with him. Then we come to the fall of Srebrenica in July of 1995. You were on leave at the time. This is covered in your original statement. The attack intensified in -- on Srebrenica intensified on the 8th, 9th, 10th, and 11th of July. That also is covered in your statement. There are then some exhibits that you can produce but we'll deal with them very briefly. Tab 13, have you reviewed that? Is that a code cable dealing with the position on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it's a code cable from the headquarters in Zagreb, an Akashi code cable reviewing the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the accused saying that he understood that it may be necessary for close-air support to be used, stating that General Mladic might not understand the difference between close-air support and airstrike.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And warning of the possibility of Mladic reacting strongly.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit tab 14, is that another code cable for the 11th of July that you've reviewed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the accused made contact, was briefed on the situation, and said that the Netherlands' soldiers in Serb-held areas retained their weapons and equipment were free to move about?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally tab 15, a code cable for the same day, which includes the passage that "The BSA is likely to separate the military-age men from the rest of the population, an eventuality about which UNPROFOR troops will be able to do very little." Does it go on to say that "The fact that the Bosnian Serb Army will have practical difficulties controlling 40.000 people may mitigate against their desire to prolong or exacerbate the plight of the Srebrenica population"?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I remember reading that. I can't find it at the moment, but it's in here somewhere, I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's tab 15, and it's now on the screen before you. We move to paragraph 58.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is your concern for the refugee problem that was developing, and you covered that in your original statement, but have you reviewed tab 16, dated the 13th of July, a code cable dealing with the situation, which sets out that there were approximately 5.500 people displaced at the air base, that number being expected to rise, and that there were an estimated 6.000 people in Kladanj who will be going to Tuzla, many others to follow, about 25.000?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also an understanding that there were about 4.000 men of draft age in Bratunac awaiting screening by the Bosnian Serb army, their fate being of concern to everyone.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. That I can -- I recognise the code cable, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 17 is another document you've reviewed, dated the 13th of July, setting out a meeting between you and Prime Minister Silajdzic on the 13th of July. And does that contain this passage, that "Silajdzic informed General Smith that the government had held an Extraordinary Session of Parliament today and were about to release a ... list of their demands. This would include a request for the UN to reinforce the Zepa enclave. He stated that, firstly, Zepa was the immediate priority as it had become apparent that it would certainly be the next target and that Belgrade was actively involved and no longer bothered to conceal this fact." Paragraph 6 of the same document said: "Both the Prime Minister and Minister Muratovic raised their concerns about the as-yet-unconfirmed reports of atrocities in the Srebrenica area, in particular the rape of young women in Vlasenica area and the murder of a busload of refugees." Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that accurately set out --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it does, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally for exhibits at this stage, tab 18, a document dated the 13th of July you've considered. The aftermath of the fall of Srebrenica and the comment that the Bosnian Serbs clean -- cleansing Srebrenica. What do you say about that, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I wrote this document. This is me at the end of -- or at some stage during that day, I only arriving back in the late hours of the 12th of July, sending off my views as to the position we -- as to how we should approach the future, and I'm -- in there, I am producing the -- in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. situation, and I'm saying that the Bosnian Serbs are cleansing Srebrenica, by which I mean - and I'm using the word as it was being used at the time - the process of separating the men of military age from the rest of the population, and this was the normal behaviour when people captured a village or whatever during this war and in that part of the -- and in that part of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Summary page 17, paragraph 60 to 67 to be given live, and if you'd perhaps try and deal with it from recollection, referring only to any other documents if you need to and on request because it concerns the accused directly. Was there a meeting on the 14th of July between yourself, the accused, and Carl Bildt in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, there was, yes. I was hesitating over the date. Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also a meeting with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Mladic was there with Milosevic when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that date right, the 14th? I put a reference to the 15th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was hesitating because I thought it was the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My error. It is the 15th. The 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about the meeting. How did it start and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, perhaps Mr. Nice's service, which is rather large and effective, could perhaps find the document. There is the Akashi report to Kofi Annan dated Zagreb, the 17th of July, 1995, and it says: "For Annan, United Nations New York, Information on Stoltenberg ICFY Geneva from Akashi, UNPROFOR main headquarters Zagreb, number Z-1175." The date is the 17th of July, 1995, and the reference is the meeting in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And what is the date, if there's a point? What is the date that you say from that document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That document, the date is the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The date of the meeting. What is the date of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the date of the meeting is Sunday, the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the meeting at --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it is Akashi's report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the meeting outside a hunting lodge at Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can have the full people attending if necessary. Did the meeting split into military and political groups?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the military group. What happened in that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: We started with everyone together, and very soon after we started, Mr. Milosevic directed Mladic to go with me and sort out the recovery of the Dutch Battalion and access to prisoners and so forth, and we went off separately and held our meeting to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what terms did the accused instruct Mladic and with what apparent authority?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: They were -- he was clearly the superior of Mladic. He referred to Mladic by his Christian name and Mladic was deferring to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meeting you had with Mladic, in summary, how did that progress?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Slowly and in a rather combative manner, but we eventually arrived at a document which I believe you will -- you have in the pack, which became the basis of our subsequent meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's tab 20, I think, in the binder. Indeed it identifies the date of the 15th of July as the meeting.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I was referring to the one where -- which Mladic and I signed at Han-Cram, which I think is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've reviewed both of those documents?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say it was combative. This is the 17th of July --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, the 15th of July but it was combative. Anything said directly about what had been happening at Srebrenica or was there any knowledge at that stage of the number of deaths at Srebrenica or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No. I was still working on the basis that we had a substantial number of men to see, that at least 2.000 were in Bratunac, and we -- and we couldn't account -- we didn't know where to look for the balance, and that's why we were demanding access for the ICRC and the UNHCR to these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in general, looking both forward and back if you can, at any stage was Mladic to make any acknowledgement about the number of deaths in Srebrenica or to express shock or any other emotion about what in due course it was known may have happened there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, he didn't, and I -- at this meeting, although for a more general reason, and then subsequently I made this point I'm about to tell you about, on other occasions when it was clear that these massacres had taken place, I was trying to impress upon him that the actions he was taking were damaging his position and that of his people, because they were being viewed and putting him in a very bad light. And he had no understanding, in my view, of the effect he was having on the world by the actions he was taking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the meeting with you, did he refer to the vulnerability of his own mother, I think?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently, according to him, a bomb, when we bombed Pale, had fallen within a kilometre of her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've dealt already with paragraph 65 of the summary where you've explained your view of the accused's control over Mladic. You make something that's not in your statement, an observation about the exercise of power generally in the Balkans and the degree to which subordinate authority holders have independence. Can you just explain that in a couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I came to the view quite early on that power was exercised in the Balkans as a society in the way that I called all power was absolute, and whoever had it exercised it absolutely. If you were running a roadblock, then you were all-powerful, and if you demanded goods, money, tax, or whatever, that was yours to take. Your superior only became involved if the consequence of this affected his affairs and doings, and he would only intervene in your exercise of power on that account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How if at all does that view of yours feed into your judgements about Milosevic and Mladic from what you were told and what you saw?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think that was the relationship. Mladic had his own place to exercise power and to do so, and only when this interfered with the business of Mr. Milosevic and Serbia did he get interfered with or controlled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mladic offer you an explanation about the fall of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: He told me that it had fallen long before it did, but the reason for him attacking it, we never discussed it, and it fitted with what I'd been expecting him to do anyhow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should have -- I jumped over a couple of passages. You've dealt in your statement with the agreement on the evacuation of DutchBat. You've reviewed Exhibit 21, which we've already considered. And I should have got you to make clear that Mladic had reported to you that Srebrenica was finished in a correct way as you set out in your original witness statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We come to the fall of Zepa. Did he show you a map at the time he was dealing with that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. And he was endeavouring to get a -- the local representatives to deal with him at the time, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had a further meeting with Mladic on the 25th of July at Han-Cram; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Covered in your statement. You spend four hours with him, and that's also dealt with in your statement. You've reviewed an exhibit, tab 22, which sets out a record of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And that's a record of it. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Included in that, I think, you met -- in that meeting you met Bosnian officials, ICRC staff, and some UN civil affairs staff?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, what happened is I met them on the road, and I was trying to get these people into Zepa in order to be sure that we weren't about to have another Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think -- did you form a view as to whether you were going to be able to resist cleansing of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: We -- we were not going to be able to prevent the evacuation of the people in the enclave. The important thing was to get them out safely. There was a -- the -- whether or not the armed people in the enclave at that stage were going to be able to extract or they would go off into the hills wasn't clear. Eventually they went off into the hills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make efforts to get them registered as well?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Registered the people who had been taken so that we could account for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had a further visit to Zepa between the 26th and 29th of July covered in your witness statement. And Mladic was keen to exchange prisoners, also dealt with in your witness statement. It was an all-for-all exchange, I think, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. The -- I was -- became something of a negotiator at that stage of carrying the message between the Bosnian government and Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Deal with what else happened in Zepa, the Bosnian army's refusal to surrender in your statement. By the 30th of July, Mladic's attention had been diverted from Zepa by the start of the Croatian offensive in Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noted at the time, so far as Zepa was concerned, the appearance of some different organisation or force; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- the troops actually conducting the assault into Zepa were clearly of a different organisation to those more regular Bosnian Serb soldiers on the outer cordon. These men wore black uniforms. I don't recall the colour of their head gear. Many had Serbian army flashes on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you also noticed something about the vehicle that Mladic was using at one stage.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there was two captured vehicles. One was an Ukrainian APC, still in its white colours. The other was a captured British APC, a Saxon that had been painted camouflage, and it came from Gorazde when hostages were taken there in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally on the black uniformed groups, did you notice them once or more than once? Did you notice their disappearance and infer where they'd gone?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: They were there all the time until the my last time of going there when Mladic had also gone because of the break out of fighting in the -- on the other side in Western Republika Srpska, and I deduced that these forces had gone with Mladic to reinforce the situation there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You deal, indeed, with further material on that topic. Your meeting with Mladic at Mrkonjic Grad on the 31st of July in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think your view that Zepa was not high on Mladic's agenda from this time or at this time is dealt with at paragraph 101 of your original statement. And you've reviewed tab 23, which sets out the record of your meeting of the 31st of July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have, yes. That is the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: August 1995 you cover in your original statement both as to the general position, the Lake/Holbrooke initiative, your meeting with Mladic on the 22nd of August at Borika near Zepa to discuss the withdrawal of British and Ukrainian troops; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then paragraph 82 of the summary, your original statement Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. deals with your tackling Mladic on Srebrenica, the allegations and the atrocities, and this is where you, as you've told us already, found that he didn't understand the world perception of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You raised with him the Bosnian Serb refusal to allow UNPROFOR to use the route to Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in respect of that and why, do you think?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- my memory is that he then said he'd lift the restrictions. The -- and this, as it were, was something of a quid pro quo for the UNHCR help that we'd got across to deal with the refugees that were flooding into Banja Luka and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two more very short topics, although each of them not necessarily small in significance. First, the foreseeability of the massacre at Srebrenica. You told us that you -- this is page 23, paragraph 84. You told us that you were on leave when the attack on Srebrenica began. You've told us about your original thesis and your expectation of a squeezing on the safe areas. So far as you were concerned, were you surprised or otherwise when you learnt of the scale of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I was -- was extremely surprised. I had not expected that to have happened at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it fit with, not fit with your thesis or does it constitute a separate event?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think it is a separate event. The thesis was sufficiently accurate to suppose that this squeezing would take place, and indeed that was the basis of the interpretation of the events that led up to the collapse of the pocket. In the aftermath, you get these murders, and that was not -- I just did not consider that that would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 24 of the summary, paragraph 89. Just yes or no, were you able to form a view about whether Milosevic had any knowledge after the event of the killings at Srebrenica? Just yes or no to that.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did form --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is how were you able to form a view before I invite you to offer it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Because of the meeting that took place on the 15th of July, there must have been -- he must have understood - and he had Mladic there - they must have known what had gone on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The last topic, Markale II as it's described, that is the mortars going into the old town on the 28th of August and the killing of the 37 and wounding of 88 people outside the Markale marketplace. Was there an investigation into that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The nature of the investigation? Who caused it to happen?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- the -- any mortaring, any shelling, the UNMOs automatically carried out an investigation and recorded the data they collected. This was of such significance that particular attention was paid to this particular attack, and because I wanted to be absolutely sure that all the data had been collected, I had a second iteration of this investigation in which a -- my senior intelligence officer was instructed to collect all the information available. He didn't exactly carry out the investigation himself; he assembled all the data, and it was on the basis of that that I came to my decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your decision was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That beyond reasonable doubt these rounds had come from the Bosnian Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify the elements of the investigation or the report following the investigation that led to your forming that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The crater analysis gave a direction. The -- and the nature of the weapon systems. The observation post reports, whether they'd heard weapons fired or not, told us whether they'd been fired or not from within the siege as opposed to without. There was an acoustic system which was also interrogated to see whether they'd picked up anything in the city. It had not. And then there was the radars, and they too, by negative information, you were able to exclude certain possibilities. While no one had actually seen the mortars fired, equally they hadn't seen any of the other evidence of it being fired from inside of the siege. On that basis, I came to that conclusion that this had been fired from outside the siege.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've reviewed two exhibits, tabs 24 and 25 covering this. One a code cable from the office of the commander to the HQ UNPF in Zagreb, the mortar incident report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at tab 25, a document headed "Sarajevo Firing Incident." Any comments you want to make on those?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the -- if I remember how it was done, the bureaucracy of it, the first document is the -- is collecting all together the various reports, the UNMOs, reports and so forth which are annexes to that first report, and the subsequent one is the memoranda from the intelligence officer, Powers, where he pulls together all these reports under the one -- under the one cover and presents them to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As summarised, your tour of duty ended in December. But that's all I wish to ask you. You will be asked some further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Could I remind you, as we remind all witnesses, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. If you would be back in 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice needed an hour and a half just to skip through all these documents. I do not believe that I can cross-examine this witness within the rest of the time today, and I don't think that General Smith could not come perhaps again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: More precisely, the Prosecution took an hour and a quarter rather than an hour and a half. You've got the rest of the day, so let's see what progress we can make. I advise you not to waste any time with argument and the like.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no intention of wasting time, Mr. May. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us begin with what the examination-in-chief ended by Mr. Nice and which General Smith commented on. Namely, last night I received a document in accordance with the practice for me to be given documents at the last moment. It doesn't have an ERN number. It just says the 8th of October, 2003, and in the accompanying letter in connection with witness Rupert Smith, pursuant to Rule 68, information report, information provided by Brigadier J. Baxter of the British army to Mark Ierace, et cetera. It refers to Markale, the shelling incident, on the 28th of August, 1995. I don't know whether you have that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I don't know what you're talking about. Mr. Nice, can you help us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It was a document provided under our wide comprehension of Rule 68 and is indeed an information report provided by Brigadier Baxter of the British army to officers of the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm not sure if it's document you want. I'm sure if it becomes material, we can copy it and make it available to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think it should be done. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You can ask some questions. Certainly, Mr. Nice, the witness should have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has a copy, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Smith, he says: "My tour of duty was January to November [In English] 1995. I was MA to Smith throughout." MA, military assistant, I suppose. [Interpretation] And at the end of that first paragraph which is headed "In relation to the Markale shelling incident of the 28th of August," he says: "[In English] My original thought at that time was that this was two different attacks from two different locations - from two different directions, one from inside the lines." [Interpretation] And then he says: "[In English] When we went back to UN headquarters there was initial talk of the killing round being fired by the Bosnians. The information from the French was that the round could have been fired from within the lines. This was from the first analysis of the UNMOs and the French. It did not appear from verbal reports that there had been two attacks because the rounds were said to be within seconds." [Interpretation] Then in the next paragraph, it says, in the third line: "Considering the reports of the UNMOs and of the Sector Sarajevo French engineers, [In English] we were troubled at the lack of correlation between the information reported." [Interpretation] And at the end of the paragraph mention is made of the fact that you designated Colonel Powers to investigate. And at the end of the paragraph, it says: "Powers provided a subsidiary report [In English] that afternoon that became the basis for the general's decisions." [Interpretation] And then on page 2, in the fourth paragraph, it says: "[In English] The UNMOs reported one thing and the French engineers something else."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were three opinions: The UNMOs, Sector Sarajevo (French engineers) who had access to the Cymbelline" - [Interpretation] I don't know what that means - "the OP reports, and UNPROFOR." Cymbelline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. The general should have a chance to deal with all this, because if we go too far, it will be impossible for a witness to be able to answer. We will return to the meaning of OPs and the like. General, can you comment on the statement, as I understand it to be, which was made by the brigadier, or his comment in the statement, about the initial reports and the reports from the French, and then we'll come on to the reports of the UNMOs and the French engineers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I've only got on to the second page of this document, so I'll get that far. The -- as I said before we adjourned, the UNMOs would have done an investigation as a matter of course. The responsible sector commander -- the UNMOs were a separate organisation, and the Court may know this, but reporting direct to Zagreb. They were not under my command, although they had a liaison officer and I knew what they were saying to Zagreb. The Sector Sarajevo, who is the responsible commander for the vicinity, would have also carried out investigation and would normally have done this together with and in cooperation with the UNMOs. Because there was confusion in the reporting and I needed an answer, I needed to know who had perpetrated this, I directed that my own staff officer, Colonel Powers, to carry out a further investigation and to gather together all these reports so that we could reconcile them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Court has now got a copy of what's described as an information report. The other matter you can help us on, General, is the OP, observation posts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And Mr. Milosevic is correct; an MA is a military assistant. He is the senior personal staff officer to a commander, and Colonel Baxter, as he was then, fulfilled that role at that time for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then he says: "My recollection is that UNMOs report was adamant that there were two firing points [In English] Theory, but the UNPROFOR report thought that it was one." [Interpretation] And then in the next paragraph but one, it says: "The deputy commander of Sector Sarajevo (a Russian colonel) -" then there's a question mark there and I don't understand why - "publicly claimed the Bosnians had fired the killing round. [In English] UNHQ said we needed further investigation as the deputy commander had gone public and the matter had to go before the Security Council." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. [Interpretation] And then next it says: "At this time, there was almost a mutiny. [In English] UNHQ forced the need for the report on us because of the press interest encouraged by the Serbs. The deputy commander went on TV. He insisted that it could not have been the Bosnian Serbs. He resigned as a result of the position that he took."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pause there. General, is that correct? Can you help as to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The thing that I'm missing from this report is a sense of chronology, and my memory, and it's only that, is that I had come to my decision and we were already acting on it when we're being asked to render further reports as a result of the sector Sarajevo's deputy commander, who was a Russian colonel, had said what he'd said on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in the last paragraph on that page, it says: "Almost immediately after the attack [In English] Admiral Smith --" [Interpretation] it's the same name but he was commander of the southern sector of -- "turned the NATO key." He turned the NATO key for bombing. There were two keys, one with the UN, the other one with NATO, and the NATO key was turned by this witness, General Smith. Isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I did not turn the NATO key, no. I turned the UN key.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Admiral Smith turned the NATO key, and you turned the UN key; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct. What is not correct, in my opinion, is that he did it almost immediately after the attack. I'd have to go and find out the actual, but I'm sure it's on the record somewhere. It happened -- there was discussion as to who do it before Admiral Smith turned his key, in my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, Admiral Smith, the expression being "turned the key," he actually decided that the bombing start even before he had a precise report as to who had done it. Isn't at that right, General Smith?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't think that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the decision for you to turn the key was yours. And then it says: "Mladic and Smith" - Smith this time being you - "had a phone conversation. Mladic promised to investigate, and wanted a joint investigation of the UN and the Serbs. [In English] This forced a quick decision." [Interpretation] And then it says: "As to legitimate military targets within the confrontation lines, there were no static facilities, however, the ABiH maintained a mobile mortar which would be driven into position, fired, and moved on. ... [In English] The Serbs complained quite a lot about these mobile mortars and about us telling them not to fire at these mortars." [Interpretation] And then he says: "[In English] Serb attacks would sometimes be a 'cause and effect' phenomenon; in response to an incident somewhere on confrontation lines, they would reply in force. Bosnians killed two people at a funeral or wedding the day before. Indeed, I cannot recall a Serb attack which did not have its genesis in response to something linked to the ground. For example, I recall an attack explained by the Serbs as the ABiH attacked in Bihac so the Serbs responded to be -- by shelling Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where are you reading from, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3, first, second, third -- fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received it in the original in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it says in the next: "[In English] Markale attack seemed unprovoked, did not seem linked to anything else."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The general can deal with that comment, if he wishes, of course. Is there anything you'd like to add to that, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember if there was a linking effect. It is true there was usually -- you could usually follow some cause and effect somewhere. I don't remember if there was an obvious one or not on this occasion at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the last sentence in the next paragraph says: "In the days following the UNMOs said it was difficult to tell who was responsible." And then let me skip over a paragraph to save time. The next one says: "[In English] There was significant American pressure through NATO to begin bombing as soon as possible. French had grave reservations about the bombing taking place - delicate position. Smith consulted with Sector Sarajevo but they would not have known he was going to turn the key."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. General, perhaps you can deal with that paragraph, the reported views, as they seem to be, of Brigadier Baxter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't recall it in quite -- with quite the sense of that paragraph. Yes, there was questions from NATO. I don't recall any -- this being of particular American flavour, although clearly the Americans are in NATO. There was nothing at the time, as I remember it, from the American embassy, and normally when you knew you were -- NATO was being used by the Americans in those cases, then you got it from the American embassy as well as through NATO. Nor do I remember any more than the argument that has been disposed here. We had conflicting views. I was needing to, as I came to a decision myself, reconcile these reports. I don't remember the French being -- having the reservations as laid out in that position. They had produced a report, and that was their view at the time, rather than it was quite as strongly put in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then in one of the following paragraphs it says: "G2 reports to the Chief of Staff, who was brigadier - he was with Powers when he briefed Smith - I produced the report because it had become a political issue. [In English] The British SNCO was only the technical advisor. I recall almost protesting having to sign off on the report - being put in a position to do this." The last sentence in this report says: [In English] "... in my view. When I wrote the report there was still doubt in my mind."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just read on. If we are going to do this, you must read the whole paragraph. "What convinced me was the fuse furrow." Perhaps, General, you can help us with that. This gentleman is saying he was equivocal. There was doubt when he wrote the report, which of course is the report which we have, which we've got in our documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "What convinced me," he says, "was the fuse furrow." Since he's not here to speak about it himself, perhaps you can interpret that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When a -- let's just deal with a mortar round hits the ground, it comes in at a fairly -- usually at a fairly steep angle. It's -- the leading point is the fuse. And you get a crater shape that looks a bit like a bat or an outline of a bat, and if you -- with the shrapnel being driven down from the inside the narrow angle of the vertical -- from the horizontal, where the round has come in is a dense hole, then you get the bat wings from the side of the round where it's exploded and the shrapnel going out more or less horizontal with the ground and then you've got the bit, as it were, on the upside of the slope as the round has come in and has gone up in the air and you don't get that mark on the ground. And on the leading edge of that there is a very thin edge which is called a fuse furrow. And if you want to get a bearing, a direction from which this round has come from, then you examine the fuse furrow and follow the fuse furrow down into the ground and lay a stick on it and so forth, and then you can start to work out where this round might have come from, and it would have been that analysis that was convincing of him, and I believe that had been carried out by either the UNMOs and/or the British artillery NCO that worked for General Powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
