utterances.text: I think the witness has dealt with all this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move on to my next question then. You know that in the report of the Dutch government, dated April 2001, in paragraph 10, it says literally: "There are no indications whatsoever that the action was carried out in cooperation with Belgrade in the sense of political or military coordination." Is that right, General Smith?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know. I've not read the report to that detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about that, that anyone from Serbia or Yugoslavia in any way whatsoever was involved in those events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No. I have no direct personal knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then tell me, please, as you say this on page 3, paragraph -- page 9, paragraph 3 of your statement, that Mladic explained to you that he was expecting a Bosnian attack from the eastern enclaves, and he told you that in that case, he would attack the enclaves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there attacks from the eastern enclaves that we referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I told you there were those patrols and raids.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 10, paragraph 3, you refer to the 13th of March in Pale where there was a meeting with the leadership of Republika Srpska. You mention Karadzic, Koljevic, Krajisnik, and Mladic, and then you say that the atmosphere of the meeting was marred by the shooting of two Serb girls in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, at the time regarding freedom of movement and humanitarian aid, did Mladic insist on reciprocity, and did he complain of the constant activities of the Bosnian government forces in the enclaves and other safe areas that you referred to on page 10, paragraph 3 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: He did ask for reciprocity, and he did complain of the activities of the Bosnian forces in the enclaves, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything done at the time for a reciprocal respect to be ensured of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, the unnecessary activities on both sides to prevent raids from the safe areas or anything like that? Did you undertake anything? Did UNPROFOR do anything? What was the material consequence of those discussions and agreements?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: We were working extremely hard through the joint commission, and Mr. Akashi at the political level, to try to make this Cessation of Hostilities Agreement work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what was happening at the military level?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I told you. That's where the joint commission worked. It was unfortunate that the -- General Mladic would not attend the joint commission and was refusing some of his officers to come to the meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who came on behalf of the army of Republika Srpska to those joint commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: My memory is that we -- the process broke down because neither parties would come to the meetings in the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the situation continued to deteriorate in the following week when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina launched an offensive along two axes, and I draw your attention to page 10, paragraph 5 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure. My page 10 has paragraphs 41 to 45 on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably 42.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got it. I quote: "Matters continued to deteriorate during the following week." Is that the one you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, because the Bosnian army mounted an offensive in two directions.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, matters did deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they deteriorated due to the activities engaged in by the Muslim side; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. On page 11, paragraph 3, you refer to a meeting on the 5th of April with Karadzic, that you heard that the Bosnian Serbs felt that they were betrayed by the former US President Carter, by the United Nations and the international community, and Karadzic simply said, "We will respond to attacks where we are attacked." So didn't threaten anyone. He just said he would return fire where they were attacked.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't find that on page 3 in my -- beg your pardon, page 11, paragraph 3. Where are we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about paragraph 46. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Okay. Let's try -- I mean, there I'm reporting that Karadzic said that the Bosnian Serb army would not respect the safe areas and claimed them to be illegal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please look at the last sentence of paragraph 45.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've found the reference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say there, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: You want me to read out the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you have just found.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I will. "He asked -- he took the opportunity to deliver a message to me in the knowledge that I would pass it on. The message was that the Bosnian Serbs had decided that the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement had failed and that the Bosnian Serbs felt that they had been let down by former US President Carter, the United Nations, and the international community. He made it clear that they had made a decision, that is the Bosnian Serbs, to carry out a counter-offensive again the Bosnians. Karadzic accepted that this is likely to bring the Bosnian Serbs into confrontation with the UN and NATO. Karadzic did not divulge the form of this offensive but simply said, `We will counter-attack where we have been attacked.'"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where they are attacked, they will counter-attack. That's what he said. That's the gist of this, isn't it, of what he's saying? Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I -- I -- I suspect that I am reporting verbatim what he said. It's more than the gist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since you speak about fighting around Sarajevo and in Sarajevo, as your sources of information, you used, as you say, primarily the warring parties themselves. You say this on page 23, in the second, third, and fourth paragraphs. The point is that you used as your source the information from the warring parties themselves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not exclusively. I'm trying to find the -- where's the reference? I'm on page 23. Mr. Milosevic, would you give me the first sentence of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have it here. I just noted down that you referred to this on page 23, in the second, third, and fourth paragraph, but I'll find it straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know that we're going to find this, and time is now moving on, so either ask a general -- just ask a general question or move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. According to your information, you gathered various information about the events in Sarajevo and in the theatre of war around Sarajevo. Do you know how many Serbs were killed in Sarajevo during the war in the period from 1992 to 1995? Did you ever receive this figure, and did you ever ask for it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Whether I asked for it directly or it was provided for me anyhow, I don't recall, and I'm sure I had that information available to me. I do not remember the figure now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it ring a bell if I remind you that there were about 10.000 killed Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, that doesn't -- the figure doesn't help me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the fate about 5.000 Serbs from Sarajevo is still not known, Sarajevo and the surroundings?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't know those figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how many Serbs were forced to leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Close to 150.000. You don't know anything about that figure?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not at that point in time, but if we have these figures in mind, I mentioned 10.000 killed and 150.000 expelled, you spent a whole year without interruption there. Could you tell me to what extent the suffering of the Serbs figured in your reports, assessments, and everything else that you produced?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: A great deal. I was as concerned for their condition as I was for everybody else's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question, Mr. Milosevic. We will then give Mr. Tapuskovic five minutes if he would like to ask some questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me, General, please, do you have any knowledge at all about Radovan Karadzic ordering units to halt the shelling, to stop sniping, to react proportionately, endeavouring as much as he could to calm down the situation around Sarajevo, which was the hot point, the hottest point? I'm just asking you whether you have any knowledge about that at all. And he did so on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not specifically. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Before we go on, we'll deal with the two documents which the accused referred to. The one was the Information Report provided by Brigadier Baxter to members of the OTP. That is not a document which we shall admit in evidence. It is, insofar as it is a statement at all, it's one which we have consistently refused to admit. If the accused wishes, he can call the witness to give evidence. The other document is a different category. It is another information report, but on this occasion it is provided by the witness himself, which puts it in a different position since he's here giving evidence and has been able to answer questions about it. Mr. Milosevic, do you want the information report of the witness to be admitted? You put a passage in it to him. Do you want it admitted or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you didn't let me finish my last question, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Milosevic. I said you had one last question and you had it. Now, let's have Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it contains an exhibit, this last question, because I have here a copy of an order signed by Radovan Karadzic about the implementation of the rules of international war law in the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 13th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look at that document. It's the 13th of June, 1992, I note. I don't suppose the witness would have seen it. I don't know what language it is in. It's in B/C/S. We'll mark it for identification. We'll give it the next defence number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It will be D193.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Now, Mr. Tapuskovic, time is against us, but if you would like to take up five minutes, do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Your Honours, let me try and make the best of that time Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in your statement that has been admitted into evidence, on page 22, paragraph 2 of the English version, you said that in the evening of the 28th of August, that is the same day when the incident occurred, you took a decision together with the commander-in-chief of Sector South to launch the bombing campaign; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Can I have the paragraph number again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 22, paragraph 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay. I have it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say on page 23, paragraph 2 - turn the page please: "The unfolding of the air/land plan," as it was called, "fell into two parts. The first lasted from the 29th of August to the 1st of September. Attacks were carried out to achieve air supremacy and to show the extent and nature of the punishment." Is that right? Was that the purpose of the operation which you ordered?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: You should complete the sentence to, "The nature of the punishment to come, and to destroy weapons, command and control, and weapon dumps." Yes, I made that decision, and that was the purpose of the first part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The second part, could you explain why was it necessary, a few days later, and this bombing went on from the 5th to the 14th of September, and it was obvious that the Croats and Bosnians were taken advantage of the attacks to attack Western Bosnia and Ozren. Did the Bosnian and Croats take advantage of the air attacks for their own operations? Was that the purpose of those attacks or not?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No. The attacks continued into the second phase because the requirement to remove the weapons and so forth from around Sarajevo had not been carried out. And that was set out in another letter, as I recall, sent to the -- to General Mladic while the first part was being carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look now on page 24, paragraph 3. On the 10th of October, as it says here, upon your request NATO attacked Serb positions on Mount Vis in retaliation. You use the term "retaliation." This was in October 1995. Could you describe the circumstances under which this took place?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. The headquarters of my forces in the Tuzla area was being shelled from that vicinity, and in spite of requests for them to stop, and we had a soldier killed, I retaliated by means of bringing those airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, could you please look at the information report drafted on the 28th of August when you spoke about what was happening -- what had happened at Markale, and could you please focus on page 5, paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Do I have the -- page 5?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 5, first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It starts with "Baxter"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. And it ends with these two sentences, but this is something you didn't look at a moment ago when you made your decision. Since you were convinced up to a point, that is what you said, and then you took the decision you did by not accepting the first report compiled by an UN commission. So it was on the basis of your conviction, a certain conviction that you had.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. The -- what bit are you referring to me in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last sentence or, rather, the one before last, and the last sentence, because you didn't accept the UN report because up to a certain point, you were convinced. That is at least the translation we have. Wouldn't it be necessary for you to be absolutely convinced?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it -- I don't quite understand how these information reports are done. Are these a verbatim report of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Maybe it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the conversation but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suspect they're not. They're probably made up after the event. But in any event, it's your evidence which matters. What it says is, "There is not endless time to make a decision. I needed to make a decision by selecting a course of action based on some certainty in my mind. That is why I did not accept the first report."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have -- to understand that remark you have to read this whole conversation about the shelling, and the point I'm making is that I was receiving these conflicting reports, and I needed to arrive at an understanding and a decision of my own, and that's what I'm referring to there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think there's a matter of some problem in translation, but, Mr. Tapuskovic, could you kindly conclude your examination. We have to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had to ask questions in this connection, though I had a much more important topic to raise, but let me conclude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have in mind two substantive circumstances contained in the UN report of the 28th and the 29th when there is reference to the azimuth under which the shells were fires and in which precise data are given, that the first shell which resulted in strategic consequences was fired from a position of 170 degrees magnetic azimuth and that the other shells were fired from a completely different position with an azimuth, magnetic azimuth of 220 degrees? These are precise data which had to be respected and which showed that the shells were fired from two different positions. Did you have this in mind? Because in the report signed by Powers, certain anomalies are referred to and certain conclusions drawn which are not of an exact nature.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think -- at what point am I holding this in mind, when I'm making this comment in this information reported or whether -- when I am actually considering the matter eight years ago?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. This is information that is contained even in Lieutenant Colonel Powers' report, but he makes a certain interpretation. It is the report on the basis of which you made your decision. Even he refers to these differences in the azimuths, and these are very precise data.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think if you go back into the Information Report that I believe you're holding in your hand and look at the earlier part of this section on the -- this decision, you will find a paragraph that starts "Another crater analysis was done." And that was part of me trying to bring some clarity for the -- over these anomalies in which from one salvo you appeared to have a single round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is precisely what I'm referring to. These are anomalies that you accepted, and these data are to be found in the document signed by Powers, and those anomalies are mentioned even in that report. There was no doubt about it. Even in that document, on the basis of which the decision was made to start the operation, that data figured there too, but the explanation that was accepted was that this was some sort of a missile with anomalies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the last point that Mr. Tapuskovic is going to make. General, if you want to reply, do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't really understand your question. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have four one-liners, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One-liners literally. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How important, in your judgement on Markale, was the absence of sound from the position where the mortars were coming from?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: A very important factor, because a 120-millimetre mortar makes quite a noise when it's fired off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to presence at Srebrenica, in your meeting with Mladic, dealt with at page 17, paragraph 81 of your statement, did he indeed acknowledge after the event being at Srebrenica because he said he was just missed -- just missed being hit by a shell?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: He -- he did say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he who -- in respect of command responsibility, he who pays the cheque is usually in command. The accused raised a point about personnel administration. He who pays the cheque is usually in command. Does that mean for the soldiers in your experience working in other countries but if they're paid by their home country that there will be some command responsibility lying with their home country?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In my own experience, yes, where I have been in a similar situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Instructions to Mladic you deal with in your statement at page 17, para 79. You speak of the accused instructing him and you speak of a pre-cooked plan. Is that still your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Can I have the reference again? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 17, para 79 of your statement. Pre-cooked deal, sorry.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I believed those two had already worked out the basis of what we were going to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the accused instructed Mladic to negotiate with you as you described?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last question: Was the presence of Bosnian Serbs in the suburbs of Sarajevo of significance, in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Very, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all, and I have two matters to assist the accused in the preparation of witnesses if I can mention those, only because I shan't be here next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. General, that does conclude your evidence. Thank you for coming to give it. You are, of course, free to go. We will just deal with one or two administrative matters while you do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a letter of witnesses for the next two weeks. It's being distributed to you already and it's coming to the accused. I shan't be here next week so I hope that if there are any substantive procedural matters they can be put back to the following week. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Next week is the witness Milanovic followed by 92 bis witnesses. The week after, all things being well, we will start with C-028. There is likely to be two witnesses listed who will be short witnesses, and we then go on to C-062. For C-028, what's still called a proofing summary, in English, will be served today with a B/C/S version I hope by Tuesday of next week. That summary will be signed -- that summary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just make sure the accused has got this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is coming to the accused. It's designed to help his preparation. So it's on the second side and it's C-028. He will have the English summary today, the B/C/S will come to him sometime next week. The witness will be able to sign it on return at the beginning of the following week, and I shall be asking for that document to stand as a witness statement. So far as C-062 is concerned, there is already a signed summary, and it's been served or is -- has been served or is being served today in English and in B/C/S on the accused, and I will be asking for that signed summary to stand as a witness statement. From this stage onward, the word "witness summary" will not be used, we'll use the word "witness statement" but it happens that these were already prepared so that's the word that will be applied to them, but they are in all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I follow that last point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Never mind. But the important point is that here are some witness summaries to be prepared. We're going to ask them to stand as witness statements for the purposes of evidence in chief. And Your Honours, can we seek your assistance in relation to one procedural matter now or next week. For witnesses for whom we've applied for 92 bis, and in respect of whom you have said 92 bis but with cross-examination, if we haven't yet gone through the 92 bis procedure, may we approach the Chamber on the basis that we do with other witnesses, just witness statements, rather than weary the registry with going through the 92 bis procedure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, well, we agree to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we can follow and the accuse can hear, the first page is next week, which is Milanovic and then some 92 bis witnesses. That's the scheme. And then the week after, you will be moving on to C-028; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, C-028. And at present B-116 and Robert Franken. There was going to be another witness there but I think there are probably insuperable technical difficulties with calling that witness, so that's the present plan. And then it will be C-062. C-028 and C-062, with the leave of the Chamber, by way of signed documents for examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you can help us in order that we can deal with the calendar more expeditiously. The weekend of the 3rd -- the week, I should say, of the 3rd to the 5th, which is the week we have the witness who's been scheduled for the 3rd to the 5th, there was a problem with another witness on a Thursday. I hope that's resolved itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I still haven't heard back. We were optimistic because it was the week that that witness was looking for, and as between Wednesday and Thursday we hope there will be no difference, but we haven't yet had a reply. We will notify you as soon as we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, because there are matters which it really is important that we know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Still no contact but we're working on the basis that it's Monday to Wednesday and we'll move that witness to another day altogether if he can't make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us formally order that that week we will sit between Monday the 3rd and Wednesday the 5th of November so that everybody knows that. The other week which may cause us difficulty and out of the schedule of Tuesday to Thursday sitting is the week when there's a UN holiday, the 26th of November, which is a Wednesday, inconveniently. But apart from that, we sit Tuesday to Thursday. We will adjourn now. Apologies to the next case, please, if the registrar would pass them on.
